desecrate

/DESS-ih-krayt/ - the stress falls on DESS · verb

Hear It

What It Means

Desecrate means to violate the sacredness of a thing or place.

The trail gate closes at dusk less for safety than to keep photographers from desecrating the cliff paintings with flash rigs and fingerprints.

Example

When the army wintered in the captured city in 1644, it quartered its horses in the cathedral: hay heaped where the choir had sung, dung on the tomb slabs, muskets stacked against the font. The troopers called it convenience; their colonel meant it as a message, and both sides' chroniclers agreed the army had desecrated the place. The pews they burned that winter were furniture — the building was an altar, and everyone understood which loss was the wound.

Desecrate is the exact word for that winter, because it means to violate the sacredness of a thing or place — the target must be holy to someone, and the act insults exactly that. Vandalism breaks property; desecration breaks a promise a community made about what would be kept apart and honored.

Compare the words

Synonyms · words with a similar meaning

violate: To violate is to break in on whatever is protected — a law, a border, a trust, a quiet space. Desecrate is the special case where the protected thing is sacred: the act insults the holiness itself, not just the rule around it.

dishonor: To dishonor is to strip the respect from a person or a memory — a family name, a veteran, a promise. Desecrate needs a sacred thing or place for its target — an altar, a grave, a scripture — and the insult lands on its holiness.

What it isn’t · antonyms and near-opposites

hallow: set apart as holy

bless: ask holiness onto

Where it sits · how far beyond repair the harm goes — disturb → damage → desecrate

disturb vs. desecrate: Disturb only jostles a place — noise in the reading room, footprints on raked gravel; an apology mends it, where desecrate wounds a place's holiness past any apology's reach.

damage vs. desecrate: Damage goes further than disturb — something breaks and stays broken; desecrate claims the most: the harm lands on a place's holiness, an injury no repair crew can reach.

Build the Word

The pieces

Prefix — de-

Prefix — de-: reverse of, un-

Root — secr-

Root — secr-: sacred (Latin sacrare, to make holy)

Suffix — -ate

Suffix — -ate: to make, to do

Put it together

Put it together: De- (reverse) + secr- (sacred) + -ate = to un-sacred something. Latin sacrare made a thing holy; desecrare unmade it. The vowel shifted from sacr- to secr- inside the Latin verb family, but the meaning never moved — this is the unit's prefix doing its cleanest reversing work on the holiest possible object.

Use the root in a new word: sacred

Use the root in a new word: sacred: The islanders would not let the film crew within a mile of the sacred grove, no matter what fee was offered.

Word Choice

formal / grave

Desecrate is the strongest accusation in this unit, and it needs a sacred object to land on: graves, altars, memorials, scripture. For everyday property, vandalize; for a surface's looks, this unit's deface; for purity more broadly — a spring, a snowfield — defile. Call a parking violation desecration and you have spent the word.
